stem: A 57-year-old man with a 40-year smoking history has cough and weight loss. Serum calcium is high and parathyroid hormone is low. Chest imaging shows a 4-cm cavitating lung mass, and biopsy shows keratin pearls and intercellular bridges.
oneliner: 57M + heavy smoker + cough + weight loss + high Ca, low PTH + cavitating mass + keratin pearls → where in the lung?
ask: Where in the lung did this tumor most likely arise?

whyNot.A: Peripheral tumors are typically **adenocarcinoma**, which forms glands, not **keratin pearls** with PTHrP hypercalcemia
whyNot.B: Lymphoma arises here; it makes no **keratin pearls** or PTHrP
whyNot.C: **Mesothelioma** arises here; it shows no **keratin pearls**
whyNot.D: Lepidic growth along alveoli is **adenocarcinoma in situ**, which makes no **keratin pearls**

answer: Central, arising in a major bronchus
why: **Keratin pearls** with **PTHrP-mediated hypercalcemia** (low PTH) and **cavitation** make this **squamous cell carcinoma**. Squamous and small cell carcinomas arise **centrally** from major bronchi, while **adenocarcinoma** arises **peripherally**.

idea.rule: Squamous and small cell = central; adenocarcinoma and large cell = peripheral.
also: Squamous cell carcinoma: central, cavitation, PTHrP hypercalcemia, keratin pearls
Small cell carcinoma: central, ectopic ACTH or ADH, Lambert-Eaton
Adenocarcinoma: peripheral, commonest type and commonest in nonsmokers
Large cell carcinoma: peripheral and undifferentiated

stem: A 3-year-old boy has a 2-day history of a painful, bulging left eye with no trauma. MRI shows a 2-cm mass in the left orbit, and biopsy shows malignant small round cells, some with cross-striations, that are positive for desmin and myogenin.
oneliner: 3M + 2 d painful proptosis + 2-cm orbital mass + striated desmin- and myogenin-positive cells → which site?
ask: From which site did this tumor most likely arise?

whyNot.A: **Retinoblastoma** arises inside the globe and gives leukocoria; its cells are not **striated or desmin positive**
whyNot.B: Optic glioma or meningioma arises here; neither has **cross-striations or myogenin**
whyNot.C: Lacrimal gland tumors are epithelial, without **striated, desmin-positive** cells
whyNot.E: Metastatic **neuroblastoma** gives small round cells but they are **not striated or myogenin positive**

answer: Extraocular muscle region of the orbit (embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma)
why: **Cross-striated small round cells** positive for **desmin and myogenin** make **rhabdomyosarcoma**, a tumor of **primitive skeletal muscle cells**. It is the **most common orbital malignancy of childhood** and arises in the orbital soft tissue around the extraocular muscles; other classic sites are the **head and neck** and the **bladder or vagina**.

idea.rule: Childhood rhabdomyosarcoma = orbit, head and neck, or genitourinary tract.
also: Sarcoma botryoides: grape-like vaginal mass in girls under 5
Bladder or prostate tumors present with hematuria or urinary obstruction
Head and neck sites include the nasopharynx, middle ear and sinuses
Embryonal type is the commonest in young children

stem: A 4-year-old boy from rural Brazil has a painless tumor that has doubled in size over three weeks. Biopsy shows sheets of medium-sized B cells with a very high proliferation index and scattered pale macrophages containing debris; tumor cells are positive for EBV.
oneliner: 4M + rural Brazil + painless tumor doubling in 3 wk + starry-sky B-cell biopsy + EBV → which site of presentation?
ask: Where does this form of the tumor most typically present?

whyNot.A: The **sporadic** form presents here; an **EBV-positive** tumor in a child from **Brazil** is the **endemic** form
whyNot.C: Typical of **T-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma**, not an **EBV-positive starry-sky B-cell** tumor
whyNot.D: Contiguous nodal spread is typical of **Hodgkin lymphoma**, not a **starry-sky** B-cell tumor
whyNot.E: Typical of **mycosis fungoides**, a T-cell lymphoma of adults, not a **B-cell** tumor in a child

answer: Jaw or facial bones (endemic Burkitt lymphoma)
why: **Starry-sky** sheets of B cells with **very rapid growth** indicate **Burkitt lymphoma** (t(8;14), c-myc). The **endemic** form, seen in **Africa and also Brazil**, is **EBV** associated and presents as a **jaw or facial mass**; the **sporadic** form presents in the **abdomen**.

idea.rule: Endemic Burkitt = jaw, EBV; sporadic Burkitt = abdomen (ileocecal).
also: t(8;14) places c-myc beside the immunoglobulin heavy chain gene
Starry sky: tingible-body macrophages in sheets of B cells
Sporadic form presents as an ileocecal mass, sometimes causing intussusception
Tumor lysis syndrome can follow treatment

stem: A 56-year-old man who grew up in southern China has had bloody nasal discharge and blocked hearing in the left ear for 5 months. Examination shows a fixed, enlarged left neck node and fluid behind the left eardrum. Biopsy of a nasopharyngeal mass shows undifferentiated carcinoma positive for EBV.
oneliner: 56M + southern China + bloody nasal discharge + unilateral middle-ear effusion + fixed neck node + EBV-positive undifferentiated carcinoma → which node group?
ask: Which neck node group is this palpable node most likely in?

whyNot.A: Drain the **floor of mouth, lower lip and tongue tip**, not the **nasopharynx**
whyNot.B: Signals spread from the **abdomen (stomach)** or thorax, a distant station, not the usual node for the **nasopharynx**
whyNot.D: Drain the **arm, breast and chest wall**, not the **nasopharynx**
whyNot.E: Drain the **scalp, eyelids and parotid area**, not the **nasopharynx**

answer: Upper cervical nodes in the posterior triangle (nasopharyngeal carcinoma)
why: **EBV-positive undifferentiated carcinoma** of the nasopharynx in a man from **southern China** is **nasopharyngeal carcinoma**. It spreads **early** to the **upper cervical nodes**, typically the **posterior triangle**, and often presents as a **neck node**; a mass at the eustachian tube opening causes **serous otitis media**.

idea.rule: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma = EBV + southern China + upper posterior cervical node.
also: Risk factors: EBV, salted fish, southern Chinese or North African origin
Unilateral serous otitis media in an adult should prompt nasopharyngeal examination
Often presents first as a neck mass
Undifferentiated cells in a lymphocyte-rich stroma (lymphoepithelioma-like)

stem: A 51-year-old man who smokes and drinks daily has a firm, ulcerated mass on the tip of his tongue that makes speaking and eating difficult, with weight loss. Biopsy shows squamous cell carcinoma.
oneliner: 51M + smoker and drinker + ulcerated tongue-tip mass + weight loss + squamous cell carcinoma → which node group first?
ask: Which lymph node group is most likely involved first?

whyNot.A: The usual first nodes for **oropharyngeal** cancers; this tumor is on the **anterior** tongue tip
whyNot.B: A **late, distant** station for thoracic or abdominal spread, not first-echelon for the tongue tip
whyNot.C: Drain the **posterior pharynx and nasopharynx**, not the anterior tongue
whyNot.D: Drain the **lateral scalp and face**, not the tongue tip

why: Lymph from a squamous cancer of the **tongue tip** (**anterior oral cavity**) reaches the **submental (level IA)** nodes first. **Oropharyngeal** squamous cancers instead drain to **level II** (jugulodigastric) nodes.

idea.rule: Anterior oral cavity = submental (level I); oropharynx = level II.
also: Floor of mouth and central lower lip also drain to submental nodes
The tongue tip can drain to both sides
The lateral anterior tongue drains to submandibular (level IB) nodes
The posterior third of the tongue drains to deep cervical nodes

stem: A 52-year-old woman has a 3-cm firm mass in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast, and biopsy shows invasive ductal carcinoma. She has new mid-back pain. MRI shows lesions in several thoracic vertebral bodies, while CT of the chest and abdomen shows clear lungs and liver.
oneliner: 52F + invasive ductal breast carcinoma + back pain + thoracic vertebral lesions + clear lungs and liver → which vein carried the tumor cells?
ask: Which veins draining the breast provide the most direct route for tumor cells to the vertebral column?

whyNot.B: Drains to the subclavian vein, SVC and heart, so cells reach the **lungs** first; her **lungs are clear**
whyNot.C: Drain to the brachiocephalic veins and then the **lungs**; her **lungs are clear** despite **vertebral** lesions
whyNot.D: Joins the axillary vein, so spread goes to the **lungs**, which are **clear**
whyNot.E: Links the lateral thoracic and superficial epigastric veins in the body wall, not the **vertebral column**

answer: Intercostal veins (to the valveless vertebral venous plexus of Batson)
why: Posterior **intercostal veins** drain part of the breast and communicate directly with the **valveless vertebral venous (Batson) plexus**. Tumor cells can pass this way into the **vertebral bodies** without first being filtered by the **lungs**, which explains **vertebral metastases with clear lungs**.

idea.rule: Valveless vertebral venous (Batson) plexus = route to the spine that bypasses the lungs.
also: Prostate cancer reaches the lumbar spine through the same plexus
Raised abdominal or chest pressure can push blood into the plexus
Breast lymph from medial quadrants can reach internal mammary nodes
Intercostal veins drain to the azygos system
